Run this setup chunk first (it rebuilds `county_health` exactly as in Labs
5-7, plus the `car` package for VIFs).

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(usdata)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))

data(county_complete)
county_health <- county_complete |>
  select(
    state, name, fips, pop = pop_2019, uninsured = uninsured_2019,
    poverty = poverty_2019, median_income = median_household_income_2019,
    per_capita_income = per_capita_income_2019,
    unemployment = unemployment_rate_2019, bachelors = bachelors_2019,
    hs_grad = hs_grad_2019, median_age = median_age_2019,
    broadband = household_has_broadband_2019, density = density_2010
  ) |>
  as_tibble()

library(car)
soc <- county_health |>
  drop_na(uninsured, poverty, median_income, per_capita_income, bachelors, hs_grad)
```

# Part A: Anatomy of a collinear block (11:40-12:10)

## A1. How tangled are the socioeconomic predictors?

Compute the correlation matrix of the five socioeconomic predictors.

```{r}
#| eval: false

  select(poverty, median_income, per_capita_income, ___, ___) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```

**Which pair is most strongly correlated, and does the sign make real-world
sense?** ...

## A2. VIFs for the full model

Fit the full model and get the variance inflation factors.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_full <- lm(uninsured ~ poverty + median_income + per_capita_income +
               bachelors + hs_grad, data = soc)
vif(___)
```

**Which predictor has the largest VIF? Complete: "Its coefficient's standard
error is about ___ times larger than it would be if the predictors were
uncorrelated" (hint: square root).** ...

## A3. Watch the bachelors coefficient swing

Fit the sequence and collect the `bachelors` coefficient from each model.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m1 <- lm(uninsured ~ bachelors, data = soc)
m2 <- lm(uninsured ~ bachelors + hs_grad, data = soc)
m3 <- lm(uninsured ~ bachelors + hs_grad + poverty, data = soc)
m4 <- m_full

tibble(
  model = c("alone", "+ hs_grad", "+ poverty", "full"),
  bachelors_coef = c(coef(m1)["bachelors"], coef(m2)["___"],
                     coef(m3)["___"], coef(m4)["___"]),
  bachelors_se = c(summary(m1)$coef["bachelors", 2],
                   summary(m2)$coef["bachelors", 2],
                   summary(m3)$coef["bachelors", 2],
                   summary(m4)$coef["bachelors", 2])
)
```

**Describe what happens to the coefficient (including its sign) and to its SE
as correlated predictors enter.** ...

## A4. What stayed stable?

Collinearity destabilizes coefficients, not predictions. Check:

```{r}
#| eval: false
c(r2_m2 = summary(m2)$r.squared,
  r2_full = summary(m_full)$r.squared,
  cor_predictions = cor(predict(___), predict(___)))
```

**Complete both sentences: "If my goal were predicting county uninsured rates,
collinearity would ___." "If my goal were interpreting the bachelors
coefficient, collinearity would ___."** ...
